rationale: A wins because it keeps the founder out of fantasy land: three angles, three real tensions, all traceable to the update. Its best line, "The AI travel planner that books nothing," finds a clean contradiction without pretending the company has already changed the travel industry. B has one sharp headline, "the fare picks the destination, not the traveler," but then pads the deck with "a deal-alert brand's long reinvention," which is a profile pitch built on fumes and a former name.
gaps_in_A: "The prevailing belief, loudly marketed across the industry, is that AI agents will soon handle the entire trip end to end" is a useful frame, but it is not in the supplied facts; it needs outside evidence before anyone pitches it.
"alert-to-itinerary is a real product category" risks inflating a feature into a category. A softens it by making it a question, but the proof bar is high.
A misses the crisp behavioral inversion B found: the price signal starts the trip-planning process. That is a cleaner consumer hook than some of A's category language.
gaps_in_B: "From Scott's Cheap Flights to Going to AI trip planner: a deal-alert brand's long reinvention" is padded profile bait. The update gives a former name, not a founder arc, timeline, or reinvention narrative.

"Going is using an AI itinerary planner to convert 2 million free members into paying subscribers" asserts company intent. Premium-only supports a paywall angle; it does not prove a conversion strategy.
"a tech business reporter covering SaaS subscription models" is the wrong shelf. Going is a consumer travel membership business, not SaaS just because a subscription exists.
"earns a long-form slot" is wishcasting. Without founder access, milestone history, growth data, or internal conflict, this is not a long-form story; it is brochure scaffolding.
